extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of digital culture/media studies; researchers analyzing Internet memes and user-generated content
extracted.subtask_description: A scholarly framework for defining and analyzing Internet memes, including theoretical positions, a three-dimensional analytic taxonomy (content, form, stance), empirical methods for sampling derivatives, and distinctions between memes and virals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memetic success factors (Kilroy example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Features that help a message become a meme: a simple, easily reproducible message; public placement (ensuring many potential hosts notice it); mysterious or ambiguous meaning that invites interpretation; and actions that create an invisible bond or sense of membership among replicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Kilroy Was Here' — simple phrase + doodle repeated in public places; its ambiguous meaning made it hard to contradict and encouraged engagement as people tried to solve the mystery; reproducing it signaled membership in a 'Kilroy writers' community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility of memetic variability (hypermemetic visibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Internet, memetic variability and timelines are highly visible: a corpus of many variants is discoverable with a few clicks, making the visibility of variants an integral attribute of contemporary memes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: planking and 241543903/Heads in Freezers — hundreds of versions are easily viewable online; this 'hypermemetic' scale distinguishes online memes from sporadic pre-Internet graffiti-like memes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creator/performer centrality in memetic media
rubrics_metrics.description: In many Internet memes, the creator or uploader (often visible in videos/photos) is central: uploaders become both the meme's medium and message, so performative self-presentation and personal branding are integral to the memetic object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: assess how much a meme depends on the uploader's identity/face/body; such memes reflect 'network individualism' and strategic self-commodification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy-driven logic (attention economy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes function within an attention economy where attention is the scarce resource; items structured for easy replication have higher chances of accumulating attention and further derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators: number of derivatives is an indicator of attention; design a meme/video for easy replication to appear in platform recommendation features (e.g., YouTube suggestions). Political/activist campaigns can use replicability to promote topics ('We are the 99 percent').

rubrics_metrics.name: Social logic (networked individualism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Memetic participation allows individuals to express uniqueness while signaling affiliation to a larger network; re-creating memes constructs both individual identity and communal ties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how a meme affords dual signaling: shows creator's creativity/digital literacy while referencing a shared memetic source to indicate membership in an in-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural/aesthetic logic of participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Memes should be analyzed as cultural practices shaped by norms, genres, and historical modes (e.g., fan cultures, music covers); memes blur private/public and amateur/professional distinctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trace historical roots (e.g., music video remix cultures) and consider how genre conventions shape memetic replication and acceptable transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mentalist-driven memetic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical stance: memes are idea-complexes residing in minds and are distinct from meme vehicles; observable vehicles (images, texts, rituals) are the phenotypic manifestations of those mental memes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when focusing on internal representations and transmission of ideas; treat vehicles as carriers, not as the meme itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behavior-driven memetic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical stance: memes are behaviors, practices, and artifacts inseparable from their vehicles; the meme exists only as the observable event/text/practice and should be treated as concrete units for empirical diffusion study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for diffusion studies that analyze observable acts and artifacts; expect narrower, well-defined units and empirical tractability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusive memetic approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Theoretical stance: use 'meme' broadly for memetic information in any form (ideas, brain structures, behaviors, texts, artifacts), i.e., any copyable information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides conceptual inclusivity but may reduce analytical precision; useful when tracing many intertwining forms of imitation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three memetic dimensions (content, form, stance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Analytic taxonomy: memetic items can be analyzed across three dimensions — content (ideas/ideologies conveyed), form (physical incarnation, sensory and genre-related patterns), and stance (how addressers position themselves vis-à-vis text, codes, addressees, and other speakers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply all three dimensions when analyzing a meme; examine which dimensions are conserved or altered across derivatives to understand memetic evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance subdimension: participation structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of stance: who is entitled to participate and how participation is organized (who speaks, who is addressed, who can imitate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether participation is open or gated (e.g., dominated by a demographic) — example: 'It Gets Better' videos skewed toward young, white, able-bodied American men despite platform openness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance subdimension: keying (tone and style)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of stance: the tone/modality of communication (e.g., serious, ironic, mocking, playful) that frames how a message is interpreted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify keying in originals vs derivatives — e.g., 'Leave Britney Alone' original keyed as ultra-emotional/serious while many derivatives rekey it as ironic/parodic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stance subdimension: communicative functions (Jakobson's six)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of stance: identify dominant communicative function(s) from Jakobson's typology — referential, emotive, conative, phatic, metalingual, poetic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Leave Britney Alone' emphasizes emotive (addresser's emotions), conative (imploring viewers), and referential (facts about Britney). Use this to classify what a meme primarily 'does' communicatively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's definition of an Internet meme
rubrics_metrics.description: An Internet meme is: (a) a group of digital items sharing common characteristics of content, form, and/or stance, which (b) were created with awareness of each other, and (c) were circulated, imitated, and/or transformed via the Internet by many users.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this three-part definition as a working criterion to identify memetic corpora rather than isolated viral items; emphasizes groupness, mutual awareness, and online circulation/transformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical method for analyzing meme derivatives (sampling by visibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical procedure: to study derivative uptake, use search queries on platforms, sort results by view count, select a threshold/top-N (e.g., videos above 100,000 views), and perform qualitative analysis on the sample.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the author selected 20 most-viewed 'Leave Britney Alone' derivative videos by searching relevant strings and sorting by views; this approach balances tractability with representativeness of prominent variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation vs parody distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Not all imitation equals parody: parody involves a critical stance toward the source; imitation can be sincere emulation without mocking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate derivatives that faithfully emulate source meanings from those that reframe/critique via parody; e.g., many 'Leave Britney Alone' derivatives are parodic, reversing original stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension conservation vs mutation in derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical pattern: the form dimension is often imitated with high accuracy across derivatives, whereas content and stance tend to undergo more radical alteration (parody, reversal, reinterpretation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a corpus, check which dimensions are conserved — preserved form with altered content/stance may indicate memetic templates used for new ideological purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Memes vs virals distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Key difference: virals are single cultural units that propagate rapidly (person-to-person diffusion, great speed, broad reach); memes are collections of texts/items with variation and ongoing transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these criteria when labeling an item: a standalone widely-shared video may be a 'viral video' but only becomes 'memetic' when it spawns a corpus of derivatives sharing content/form/stance and mutual awareness (e.g., Chris Crocker's video became memetic after many derivatives appeared).

rubrics_metrics.name: Defining a meme's scope by chosen dimension
rubrics_metrics.description: The boundaries of what counts as 'the same meme' depend on whether you prioritize content, form, or stance: a content-focused definition may group different forms together; a form-focused definition may identify a format-based meme across themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit which dimension(s) you use to delimit a meme in analysis; consider intersectional definitions (theme × format) for defining meme genres.
